blocks.body:
Ramsey's theorem says that a large enough finite structure, coloured with a few colours, contains a large monochromatic piece. What if the structure is infinite? For the natural numbers the answer is as good as one could hope: colour the pairs of natural numbers with finitely many colours and there is always an infinite set all of whose pairs have the same colour. For uncountable sets the picture changes completely, and some of the most natural questions cannot be settled from the standard axioms of set theory.

The partition calculus, developed by Erdős, Rado, Hajnal and others from the 1950s on, organises these questions with one piece of notation, the arrow.

blocks.title: Just enough about infinite cardinals
blocks.body:
Two sets have the same cardinality if there is a bijection between them. The natural numbers have cardinality $\aleph_0$; sets of this size are countable. Cantor showed that the real numbers are not countable; their cardinality is written $2^{\aleph_0}$, since $\mathbb R$ is in bijection with the set of all subsets of $\mathbb N$.

We work in ZFC, the usual axioms of set theory including the axiom of choice. Under choice every set can be well-ordered, and the cardinalities are themselves well-ordered: $\aleph_0 < \aleph_1 < \aleph_2 < \cdots$, where $\aleph_1$ is the smallest uncountable cardinality. A convenient model of a set of size $\aleph_1$ is $\omega_1$, the set of countable ordinals, which is well-ordered in such a way that every element has only countably many predecessors. For a cardinal $\kappa$, $\kappa^+$ denotes the next larger cardinal.

Cantor's theorem gives $2^{\aleph_0} \ge \aleph_1$. The continuum hypothesis (CH) is the statement $2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1$. Gödel (1940) showed that ZFC cannot refute CH and Cohen (1963) showed that it cannot prove it: CH is independent of ZFC.

blocks.title: Partition arrow
blocks.body:
For a set $X$ and a positive integer $n$, write $[X]^n$ for the set of all $n$-element subsets of $X$. For cardinals $\kappa, \lambda$ and positive integers $n, r$,
$$\kappa \to (\lambda)^n_r$$
means: for every set $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$ and every colouring $c : [X]^n \to \{1, \dots, r\}$, there is a set $H \subseteq X$ of cardinality $\lambda$ such that $c$ is constant on $[H]^n$. Such an $H$ is called homogeneous for $c$. The negation is written $\kappa \not\to (\lambda)^n_r$.

In words: every $r$-colouring of the $n$-subsets of a set of size $\kappa$ has a homogeneous set of size $\lambda$. Finite Ramsey's theorem (see [[ramsey]]) says that for every $k$ there is a finite $N$ with $N \to (k)^2_2$; the least such $N$ is $R(k)$.

blocks.title: Infinite Ramsey theorem (Ramsey, 1930)
blocks.body:
For all positive integers $n$ and $r$,
$$\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^n_r.$$
That is, for every colouring of the $n$-element subsets of $\mathbb N$ with $r$ colours there is an infinite $H \subseteq \mathbb N$ all of whose $n$-element subsets have the same colour.

Induction on $n$. For $n = 1$ this is the infinite [[pigeonhole]] principle: if $\mathbb N$ is split into $r$ classes, one class is infinite.

Assume the statement for $n - 1$ and let $c$ colour $[\mathbb N]^n$ with $r$ colours. We build elements $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$, infinite sets $\mathbb N = X_0 \supseteq X_1 \supseteq X_2 \supseteq \cdots$ and colours $c_0, c_1, c_2, \ldots$ as follows. Given the infinite set $X_i$, let $a_i = \min X_i$. Colour each $(n-1)$-subset $s$ of $X_i \setminus \{a_i\}$ with the colour $c(\{a_i\} \cup s)$. By the induction hypothesis there is an infinite $X_{i+1} \subseteq X_i \setminus \{a_i\}$ on whose $(n-1)$-subsets this colouring is constant, say equal to $c_i$.

Every later element $a_j$ ($j > i$) lies in $X_{i+1}$. So any $n$-set of the form $\{a_i\} \cup s$ with $s \subseteq \{a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}, \ldots\}$ has colour $c_i$; in other words, the colour of an $n$-subset of $\{a_0, a_1, \ldots\}$ depends only on its smallest element. By the case $n = 1$, infinitely many indices $i$ share the same colour $c_i$, say all $i \in I$. Then $H = \{a_i : i \in I\}$ is infinite, and every $n$-subset of $H$ has colour $c_i$ for its least element $a_i$, which is the common colour. So $H$ is homogeneous.

blocks.title: From infinite to finite: compactness
blocks.body:
The infinite theorem implies the finite one without any estimates, by a compactness argument (second example). This kind of argument, related to compactness in topology (see [[compactness]]) and to König's lemma on infinite trees, gives no bound on $R(k)$, only its existence.

Compactness can prove more than it seems. Paris and Harrington found in 1977 a slight strengthening of finite Ramsey's theorem: one also asks that the homogeneous set $H$ have at least $\min H$ elements. This statement is true, and it follows from the infinite Ramsey theorem by compactness, but it cannot be proved in Peano arithmetic. It was the first natural example of a true statement about finite sets that is independent of Peano arithmetic.

blocks.title: Uncountable sets: where the analogy fails
blocks.body: One might hope that $\kappa \to (\kappa)^2_2$ for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, or at least that $2^{\aleph_0} \to (\aleph_1)^2_2$: every 2-colouring of the pairs of real numbers has an uncountable homogeneous set. Sierpiński showed that this fails.

Using the axiom of choice, well-order the real numbers: fix a well-ordering $\prec$ of $\mathbb R$. Colour a pair $\{x, y\}$ with $x \prec y$ red if $x < y$ and blue if $x > y$. So a pair is red when the well-ordering and the usual order agree on it.

Suppose $H \subseteq \mathbb R$ is homogeneous of size $\aleph_1$. The well-ordering $\prec$ restricted to $H$ is a well-ordering of an uncountable set, so it has an initial segment of order type $\omega_1$: elements $y_\xi$, indexed by the countable ordinals $\xi$, with $y_\xi \prec y_\eta$ whenever $\xi < \eta$.

If $H$ is red, then $y_\xi < y_\eta$ whenever $\xi < \eta$: the $y_\xi$ form a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers of length $\omega_1$. For each $\xi$ choose a rational number $q_\xi$ with $y_\xi < q_\xi < y_{\xi+1}$. The open intervals $(y_\xi, y_{\xi+1})$ are pairwise disjoint, so the $q_\xi$ are distinct, and we get an injection from the uncountable set $\omega_1$ into the countable set $\mathbb Q$, which is impossible. If $H$ is blue, the same argument applies to the strictly decreasing sequence. Hence no homogeneous set of size $\aleph_1$ exists.

blocks.title: Positive results and independence
blocks.body:
The positive counterpart is the Erdős–Rado theorem (1956): for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$,
$$(2^\kappa)^+ \to (\kappa^+)^2_\kappa .$$
For $\kappa = \aleph_0$ it says that the pairs of a set of size $(2^{\aleph_0})^+$, coloured with countably many colours, have a homogeneous set of size $\aleph_1$. Sierpiński's theorem shows that $(2^{\aleph_0})^+$ cannot be replaced by $2^{\aleph_0}$ even for two colours, so this is sharp. We do not prove Erdős–Rado here; the proof is a transfinite refinement of the least-element construction used for the infinite Ramsey theorem.

These two results already produce a statement that ZFC cannot decide:
$$\aleph_2 \to (\aleph_1)^2_2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{CH}.$$
If CH holds, then $(2^{\aleph_0})^+ = \aleph_2$, and Erdős–Rado gives $\aleph_2 \to (\aleph_1)^2_2$. If CH fails, then $2^{\aleph_0} \ge \aleph_2$, so there is a set of $\aleph_2$ real numbers, and Sierpiński's colouring restricted to it has no homogeneous set of size $\aleph_1$ (the proof above works for any set of reals). Since CH is independent of ZFC, so is $\aleph_2 \to (\aleph_1)^2_2$.

At the other extreme, an uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ with $\kappa \to (\kappa)^2_2$ is called weakly compact. Such cardinals are inaccessible, and ZFC cannot prove that they exist (if ZFC is consistent). So the simplest-looking uncountable analogue of Ramsey's theorem is a large cardinal axiom.

Exponent $\omega$ behaves differently again. One can ask for a 2-colouring of the infinite subsets of $\mathbb N$ with an infinite homogeneous set. With the axiom of choice there are colourings with none (fourth example). For colourings that are definable in a simple way, however, homogeneous sets do exist: Galvin and Prikry proved in 1973 that every Borel colouring has one.

blocks.title: Monotone subsequences
blocks.body: Prove that every sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ of real numbers has an infinite subsequence that is strictly increasing, constant, or strictly decreasing.
blocks.solution:
Colour each pair $\{i, j\}$ with $i < j$ by one of three colours, according to whether $x_i < x_j$, $x_i = x_j$ or $x_i > x_j$. By $\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^2_3$ there is an infinite set $H$ of indices on which the colouring is constant. Listing $H$ in increasing order $i_1 < i_2 < \cdots$, the subsequence $x_{i_1}, x_{i_2}, \ldots$ is strictly increasing, constant or strictly decreasing according to the colour. (Each consecutive pair has the common colour, and so does every pair.)

The finite analogue is the Erdős–Szekeres theorem: any $n^2 + 1$ distinct reals in sequence contain a monotone subsequence of length $n + 1$, and $n^2$ do not suffice.

blocks.title: Finite Ramsey from infinite Ramsey
blocks.body: Deduce from $\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^2_2$, without any estimates, that for every $k$ there is a finite $N$ with $N \to (k)^2_2$.
blocks.solution:
Suppose not: for some $k$ and every $N$ there is a colouring $c_N$ of the pairs of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with no homogeneous $k$-set. List all pairs of positive integers as $p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots$.

We build a colouring $c$ of all pairs of $\mathbb N$. Let $S_0$ be the set of all $N$. Infinitely many $N \in S_0$ have $p_1 \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$, and among them infinitely many give $p_1$ the same colour; call that colour $c(p_1)$ and the infinite set of such $N$ $S_1$. Repeat: from the infinite set $S_{j-1}$, keep those $N$ with $p_j \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ (all but finitely many); among them some colour is taken by $c_N(p_j)$ for infinitely many $N$. Call that colour $c(p_j)$ and let $S_j$ be the infinite set of those $N$. By construction, every $N \in S_j$ agrees with $c$ on $p_1, \dots, p_j$.

By the infinite Ramsey theorem, $c$ has an infinite homogeneous set; take $k$ of its elements, forming a set $K$. The pairs inside $K$ are among $p_1, \dots, p_J$ for some $J$. Any $N \in S_J$ is defined on these pairs and agrees with $c$ there, so $K$ is a homogeneous $k$-set for $c_N$, a contradiction.

blocks.title: Infinite point sets
blocks.body: Show that every infinite set of points in the plane contains an infinite subset that either lies on a single line or has no three points on a line.
blocks.solution:
Take a countably infinite subset $X$. Colour each 3-element subset of $X$ red if its points are collinear and blue otherwise. By $\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^3_2$ there is an infinite homogeneous $H \subseteq X$.

If $H$ is blue, no three of its points are collinear. If $H$ is red, fix two points $a, b \in H$; every other $c \in H$ is collinear with $a$ and $b$, so lies on the line $ab$, and all of $H$ is on that line.

blocks.title: No Ramsey theorem for infinite exponent
blocks.body: Using the axiom of choice, construct a 2-colouring of the infinite subsets of $\mathbb N$ such that no infinite $H \subseteq \mathbb N$ has all its infinite subsets of the same colour.
blocks.solution:
Call infinite sets $X, Y \subseteq \mathbb N$ equivalent if their symmetric difference $X \triangle Y$ is finite. This is an equivalence relation. By the axiom of choice, pick one representative $r(X)$ from each equivalence class, so that $r(X) = r(Y)$ whenever $X$ and $Y$ are equivalent. Colour $X$ red if $|X \triangle r(X)|$ is even and blue if it is odd.

Let $H$ be any infinite set, $m = \min H$ and $H' = H \setminus \{m\}$. Both are infinite subsets of $H$, and they are equivalent, so $r(H') = r(H) =: r$. Since $H' \triangle r = (H \triangle r) \triangle \{m\}$, the sizes $|H' \triangle r|$ and $|H \triangle r|$ differ by exactly one. So $H$ and $H'$ have different colours, and $H$ is not homogeneous.

blocks.body:
- Homogeneous means every $n$-subset of $H$ has the same colour, not merely the $n$-subsets of consecutive elements. In the proof above, the reduction to the least element is what makes the colour depend on one index only.
- The arrow relation stays true when $\kappa$ is increased or $\lambda$ or $r$ is decreased. Decreasing the exponent $n$ is safe when $\lambda$ is infinite (fourth exercise) but not in general: $3 \to (3)^3_2$ holds trivially, while $3 \not\to (3)^2_2$.
- The uncountable analogue of the infinite Ramsey theorem fails in ZFC for $2^{\aleph_0}$ (Sierpiński), and its validity for $\aleph_2$ depends on CH. Do not transfer the countable proof naively: run transfinitely, the construction reaches limit stages where the intersection of the nested sets built so far can be empty, which is one way to see why the Erdős–Rado theorem needs a much larger starting set.
- Compactness arguments prove that finite numbers exist without bounding them. The Paris–Harrington theorem shows that this loss can be essential.
- Counterexamples like the one for exponent $\omega$ use the axiom of choice; they cannot be written down explicitly.

- [[ramsey]]: finite Ramsey theory, which compactness derives from the infinite theorem.
- [[ramsey-arithmetic]]: Hindman's theorem (1974), that every finite colouring of $\mathbb N$ has an infinite set all of whose finite sums have one colour, is an infinite Ramsey theorem with a slick proof via ultrafilters.
- [[compactness]]: the passage from infinite to finite statements is a topological compactness argument in disguise (Tychonoff's theorem for the space of colourings).
- [[hypergraphs]]: colouring $n$-subsets is colouring the edges of a complete $n$-uniform hypergraph.
- [[real-numbers]]: Sierpiński's argument rests on the countable dense subset $\mathbb Q$ of $\mathbb R$.

1. Prove that every infinite partially ordered set contains an infinite chain (pairwise comparable elements) or an infinite antichain (pairwise incomparable elements).
2. Show that $\kappa \to (\aleph_0)^n_r$ for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$ and all positive integers $n, r$.
3. Prove that every infinite set of points in space contains an infinite subset that lies in one plane or has no four points in a common plane.
4. Show that if $\kappa \to (\lambda)^n_r$ with $\lambda$ infinite and $n \ge 2$, then also $\kappa \to (\lambda)^{n-1}_r$.
